title: Linear and logistic models from scratch

wrong.ols_no_intercept.py: ols_fit solves for the intercept but returns 0.0 for it, so any data not through the origin is fitted badly
wrong.ridge_penalises_bias.py: ridge_fit shrinks the intercept along with the weights, so the model drifts toward predicting 0 instead of the mean
wrong.ridge_half_lambda.py: ridge_fit adds 0.5 * lam * I: the penalty convention does not match lam * ||w||^2
wrong.sigmoid_overflows.py: sigmoid is 1 / (1 + exp(-z)) with no branch on the sign: exp overflows for large negative z
wrong.loss_naive_log.py: the loss takes log(p) and log(1 - p) directly, which is infinite or NaN for confidently wrong predictions
wrong.grad_sums_not_means.py: the gradient sums over the batch instead of averaging, so it is n times too large for a mean loss
wrong.grad_sign_flipped.py: the residual is y - p instead of p - y, so the gradient points uphill
wrong.gd_adds_gradient.py: logistic_fit adds the gradient, ascending the loss instead of descending it

hints: Normal equations: append a column of ones to X, then solve (A^T A) theta = A^T y. Use np.linalg.solve, not an explicit inverse. The last entry of theta is the intercept. For ridge add lam on the diagonal of A^T A, except the intercept's entry.

Stable sigmoid: for z >= 0 use 1 / (1 + exp(-z)); for z < 0 use exp(z) / (1 + exp(z)), so exp only ever sees a non-positive number. For the loss, binary cross-entropy simplifies to mean(softplus(z) - y * z) and np.logaddexp(0, z) is a stable softplus.

The gradient of the mean cross-entropy with respect to the logits is (sigmoid(z) - y) / n. So grad_w = X^T (p - y) / n + lam * w and grad_b = mean(p - y); the bias is not penalised. If your finite-difference check disagrees, look at the mean and the sign first.
